summary: Mission Forgotten: Explore the Moon & Mars is an interactive website that teaches students and curious explorers about the spacecrafts we have sent out into space. Each one of these machines has a story of their own. Each has clear, informative facts, history and if it’s active or inactive. You can compare historical photos using the Then vs. Now drag bar by looking at the Apollo 11 landing site from the ground and from orbit, the Lunar Roving Vehicle next to a modern rover model, and the Curiosity rover early on in it’s mission and years later. There is also an equipment map, investigation files to solve, knowledge quiz and achievements to earn. You can create and test your own Mars rover, create a digital plaque to leave your mark on the Moon or Mars and download or share it. It solves the problem by providing a clear and visual way to view real information and data from NASA. All the facts are linked to information from NASA and the concept art and imagined first person narration are labelled. The AI artwork is also labelled. This project is important as it shows how these missions still help us learn how to explore further. Making them easy to understand helps the next generation understand why these discoveries are still relevant even though the signals have stopped.
details: Mission Forgotten is an interactive online story about the abandoned spacecrafts on the Moon and Mars. It does not need to be installed, or signed up to, or use a server. The site is centered around storytelling where every device has a story to tell. A user can select their device and will hear it tell them their story in first person. This is a made up story where the rover or lander are telling the story themselves. However, the stories are based on real facts from NASA. Every device has a real story behind them. The stories can be found in the Story section of the site. The story begins by selecting your device and the story will follow. This will be delivered in first person by the device. From the Apollo landers and lunar rovers, to Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, Sojourner, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity, every device has a story. Each device has a Final Message where users can read about how their mission ended. Within the Final Transmission section users can piece together an archived transmission and watch it play out. This makes you feel more personal when they stop transmitting. Their ending has been turned into a mystery within the Case Files section. Spirit became trapped in soft soil during the Martian winter. Opportunity faced a global dust storm. Ingenuity had its final flight. Within the Legacy Timeline you can see how each mission’s findings have led onto the next. Every link says Documented or Context so we know we aren’t being told a fact. Users can move the Then vs. Now slider to compare real images. Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle and Perseverance’s test double. Apollo 11 landing site from the ground and from orbit. You can click on the rings to find out what each part is. Within the Moon and Mars Equipment Map you can view a map of all the equipment. Clicking on each pin will show you the archive for one device. Each device says if they are active or inactive. Users can design and test their own Mars rover. Finally, users can create their own digital plaque. This makes space history more accessible to everyone. The site has clear differences between facts and fiction. Concept art, AI art and made up voices are all stated. Every fact relating to a mission links to a source from NASA. The site teaches you how each mission actually ended. Some missions failed and stopped transmitting. This makes students and the curious feel like the forgotten devices still matter to them, and what we will discover next. The site was created using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. All in one file. Three.js was used for 3D elements. HTML Canvas was used for the plaque studio. PNG was used for exporting. The font Martian Mono was obtained from Google Fonts. Python was used with Pillow to create the artwork. Playwright was used for automating browser tests. Claude from Anthropic was used to help with coding, writing and creating the background artwork. These are all stated on the site. All facts and photos are from NASA Science, NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, NASA Image and Video Library and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. This project was very creative as it focused on the forgotten devices. The design is very cinematic with dark blacks, dull orange from Mars and big text. This site makes the user interact with the information. They can listen, compare, solve, create and leave a mark. It is honest about its limitations. For example, the Then vs. Now slider shows two different perspectives. I focused on accuracy and honesty throughout the site. Nothing was made up as all data and quotes are from NASA. The simulations are simple so they clearly state they are teaching models. I focused on giving credit. This site is an individual project from a student so it is not endorsed by NASA. No NASA logo was used. I focused on keeping it private. There are no logins and plaques, badges and progress are only stored on the user’s browser. I focused on making it accessible. The slider can be navigated with the keyboard. Reduce motion can be turned on. The layout has been tested on desktop and phone widths. PASTE THE PROJECT URL INTO GOOGLE CHROME TO ACCESS THE IT.
